rationale: Argument B's factual premises are sound as far as they go: budget check reports a scalar top-line and has no --by model/class axis, so the per-axis fold is new logic rather than a verbatim reuse. But its predicted defect does not follow from the spec. The reconcile identity B says is 'never established' is established by the same mechanism B concedes works for the top-line: the spec pins the per-model delta to budget.js's own per-model accumulation (mirror budget.js:1052-1058) and rebaselines tokensAtStartByModel from the open span's baseline_by_model_class (§3 step 4, §4 step 8), i.e. the same clamp/baseline shape applied per model, not a scalar-only clamp over raw per-model rows. B's failure mode — 'per-model rows derived from raw whole-session totals with the clamp applied only to the scalar' — would equally break budget.js's own per-model figure, and is exactly the rejected fork (parallel re-derivation) the spec's open-span-parity principle and §4 failure mode explicitly forbid; any disagreement there is a build-agent violation of the reuse mandate, not a spec gap. Moreover, the spec does not leave the identity unverified: §5 mandates reconcile holdouts for both axes plus a disjoint-session-id test asserting rows sum to exactly tokens_total (never more), so the hypothetical B raises is a checkable, pinned assertion, not an unestablished premise. B's alternative reading (hand-rolling a per-model clamp the spec 'never specified') is contradicted by the spec's explicit per-model fold and rebaseline steps. No concrete, checkable requirement violation is established.

Argument B's core premise — that the class-axis fold is ambiguous about pricing — does not survive the spec's actual text. The spec states the fold is 'priced per model×class before summing, so map-priced runs stay correct' (§3 and §4, stated twice), which is an implementable instruction: for each class c, the row's cost is Σ over models of (tokens[m][c] × rate[m][c]), i.e. pricing happens at the model×class granularity and only the resulting costs are summed into the single class row. B's predicted failure mode (the row being priced at a single open-span model rate) directly contradicts this explicit text rather than exposing a gap in it. B's residual point — that the §5 holdout tests assert token reconciliation but not cost reconciliation against cost_total — is at most a test-coverage nicety, not a violation of any governing requirement: the load-bearing reconcile invariant (docs/guide/cli.md:110) promises reconciliation to tokens_total, which the spec tests, and the valid-solution property (c) requires implementable fold specifications, which the per-model×class pricing instruction satisfies. No concrete, checkable defect follows from B's premises; the objection reduces to a preference for an additional cost-reconcile assertion.

Argument B advances nothing and cannot carry the case. Argument A's factual premises are largely accurate — the spec does elevate the --session-id flag to highest precedence and meter files via sessionOwnedTranscriptFiles(base, sid, runStartMs) — but the inference to a material defect does not hold. First, the traversal-read surface A describes is not new: budget check already accepts the same flag and ambient env through the identical FAFF-560 precedence and the identical sessionOwnedTranscriptFiles helper, so any confinement weakness in sid handling is a pre-existing property of budget.js, not a surface this spec creates; the governing valid-solution property (3) requires the blast radius not expand and requires economics to meter only sessions recorded in the run's own ledger, both of which the reuse mandate satisfies. Second, the spec's central principle — open-span parity via shared code, 'same code reused, not a parallel re-implementation' — means requiring economics alone to validate or confine sid would force a fork from budget.js, reintroducing the exact drift this ticket exists to close and risking the byte-for-byte single-session parity invariant. Third, the change is read-only over already-on-disk ledger data: it writes nothing and adds no new I/O (property 1), so a file-selection concern shared with the reference implementation is hardening of pre-existing code, i.e. a design preference with no checkable failure predicted by the governing requirements — the spec's stated properties name no sid-confinement requirement. Fourth, the reconstruction's undeterminable-facts section notes the actual objection evidence cited no repository paths and its specific security concern is not visible; a hypothetical traversal concern that applies equally to the untouched reference implementation cannot be a regression introduced by this spec. A's predicted consequence therefore reduces to a pre-existing condition budget check already exhibits, not a defect this spec introduces or is required by its governing properties to fix within this slice.

Argument B's factual premises hold: the spec does interpolate `session_id ?? close_source` from ledger spans into the degraded-provenance warning string with no stated escaping or length bound. But the inference that this constitutes a material defect does not stand. (1) No governing requirement or settled precedent establishes that warning strings must be escaped, that `run-ledger.json` is hostile input, or that reporting surfaces face a terminal/log-injection floor — the reconstruction explicitly marks as undeterminable whether ledger contents are attacker-controlled under any realistic threat model and whether the kernel security floors impose anything on reporting verbs beyond the settled summaries. Without that premise, 'unescaped interpolation' is a hardening preference, not a checkable requirement violation. (2) The same pattern already exists on the shipped surface: budget check and economics warnings interpolate ledger- and env-derived values into operator-facing strings today; flagging it only for the new warning is a taste call with no ground truth in the requirements. (3) Argument A correctly notes the spec offers no argued defence, but absence of argument on an unstated security property is not a defect — the valid-solution properties (read-only command, no new untrusted-input execute surface, preserved attribution gate, fail-safe degradation, unchanged blast radius) are all satisfied by the WHAT decisions as written. B's predicted consequence (escape sequences reflected into output) is concrete but conditional on an unsettled trust-boundary premise the requirements do not supply, so no bounded correction is warranted by the governing block.

The ratified precedent holds that born-verifiable DONE requires decidability plus coverage of main behaviours and named edge cases, not a 1:1 scenario per DONE item; a merely-missing dedicated scenario for an otherwise-covered behaviour would be taste-level. Argument B's objection is stronger than that and survives the bar: the cost fold is a named DONE item (§8 HOW: 'Map-pricing per-model delta folds closedSpend.byModel … so cost_total spans epochs') tied to the ticket's headline defect (under-reported COST on a resumed run), yet every §5 scenario and every entry in §8's 'From tests' list asserts token quantities only — tokens_total == 600, token-row reconciliation, warnings. Argument B's predicted consequence is concrete and checkable: a build that folds closed-span token counts into per-model deltas but prices only the open-span portion satisfies every named scenario and test while shipping an epoch-scoped cost_total — the exact defect the ticket exists to close, undetected. That makes the cost axis an uncovered main behaviour, which the precedent explicitly does not excuse (only genuinely undecidable items vs. taste-lapse are distinguished, and this item is easily decidable by a test). Argument A offers no defence. The correction is bounded: add one scenario/regression-test assertion on the existing 2-epoch map-priced fixture pinning cost_total (not just token rows) to the closed+open priced sum, and name it in the 'From tests' list.

correction.summary: In §5 and §8 'From tests', extend the map-priced resumed-fixture coverage to the cost axis: add a scenario/regression test asserting that economics' cost_total on the 2-epoch fixture equals the map-priced sum of the closed-span cost (500 tokens) plus the open-span cost (100 tokens) — i.e. all 600 tokens are priced, not only the open span — and name this cost_total-spans-epochs test in the From tests DONE list alongside the --by model/--by class reconcile tests.
correction.verification: And the map-priced cost_total equals the priced sum over all 600 tokens (closed 500 + open 100) — a build that prices only the open span's cost fails this assertion

rationale: Argument B's factual premises hold: the DONE item names day|mcp|effort|phase and §5's only coverage-warning scenario exercises --by day. But its inference fails under the governing settled precedent (born-verifiable-done-means-decidable-not-one-dedicated-scenario-per-done-item): the four axes share a single uniform code branch (economicsBreakdown step 4: 'IF axis in {day,mcp,effort,phase}: do NOT fold... presence-gated warning carries the epoch-scoping'), implemented as one set-membership check — there is no per-axis fork whose branches could diverge, so the exact OR-escape hazard the precedent requires scenarios to guard against is absent. The precedent explicitly holds that grouped fixtures covering a uniformly-handled branch satisfy the bar and that an objection amounting to 'missing a 1:1 scenario per enumerated item' is taste-level, minor at most. A build that warns on day but silently omits mcp would require the build to have written per-axis branching not specified anywhere in the spec's pseudocode, which is a deviation from the spec's named implementation, not a gap in the acceptance set the precedent demands. Argument A raises no argued defence, but under the precedent the spec's scenario set meets its own born-verifiable bar without one; no material defect is established and no correction is required.
